newsitem.title: USA: Kennecott strike supportive to copper price.
newsitem.headline: Kennecott strike supportive to copper price.

text.p: The decision by 1,800 workers on Wednesday to leave their jobs at Kennecott Utah Copper's mine and problem-hit smelter caused little initial panic in the red metal markets on either side of the Atlantic but it was supporting prices, traders and analysts said.
"It's been a long time since we had a mine strike in the U.S. and it came as somewhat of a surprise," said Fred Demler, minerals economist at E D and F Man. "It's certainly adding bullish signals."

David Rinehimer of Smith Barney said there did not appear to be any significant reaction to the strike so far. "If it appears it is going to continue for an extended period of time, then I think there will be some upward adjustment of prices," Rinehimer said. A New York broker added:"It definitely saved the market from falling several cents this morning." Kennecott said Thursday management was operating all production facilities but "obviously at a reduced level". The company and labor leaders were due to sit down later this morning for further talks.
Union officials were not immediately available for comment.
The December contract traded on COMEX was up 1.25 cents midmorning Thursday at 89.85 cents per pound.
A three-year labor deal at Kennecott expired on September 30, and the company wants a new deal containing a no strike clause.
Brokers estimated that the U.S. market would become seriously worried if the strike lasted more than two weeks.
In addition, labor talks at Phelps Dodge Corp's Chino mine in New Mexico are also unresolved, with talks due to restart in the final week of October.

Globally the market is seen to be moving into surplus although stocks are still less than a month's supply, but much of the metal removed from LME warehouses recently was destined for off-exchange depots in China, several analysts have said.
Kennecott's new $1 billion smelter has been plagued with start-up problems and was due to reach capacity of 310,000 short tons in the first quarter of 1997, a year behind schedule.
Some traders were already skeptical as to how much the smelter was producing.
Earlier this week Kennecott's president Bruce Farmer said the Garfield facility was operating at 75 percent of capacity or 19,375 short tons a month.
Traders agreed the U.S. market is generally in good shape with scrap supplies tight, forcing a greater use of cathode in production of intermediate copper products.

"If we did lose 19,000 tons a month, it does become a big deal in the U.S., but from a worldwide view, it's not much," the broker said. "Premiums on copper would go up as things would get tighter, but I am not sure actual prices on LME would go up."

COMEX copper contracts still trade higher than their LME counterparts, but a producer agent believed the strike news may forestall price levelling between the two exchanges as the physical markets move into surplus.

"I might undo some arbitrage as a cautionary move," the agent said. LME stocks in Long Beach are still over 40,000 tonnes but brokers said difficulties in taking metal out speedily continued. COMEX stocks on Wednesday stood at 18,751 short tons. -- New York Commodities 212-859-1646
